evidence.quote: Saving the price and removing the copy are separate steps. A reader can fetch $20 before the update, pause, then refill $20 after removal. The next cache hit still returns $20. Removal can also fail.

mechanisms.reason: Named API reads/fills and the explicit stale refill interleaving support causal transfer; coalescing explains reduced duplicate work.

evidence.quote: Many requests miss the same product together and repeat its database lookup. Coalescing requests lets concurrent readers share one in-progress lookup.

coherence.reason: One product record connects read reuse, keys, writes, eviction, deployment and failure; all eight card objectives are covered in prerequisite order.

evidence.quote: In this example, the database owns the product record. Losing the cached copy must not lose the product.

decisions.reason: Balances reuse, read cost and source capacity against memory, extra work, freshness and failure handling; supports declining a useless cache.

evidence.quote: If requests rarely reuse results, or freshness is too hard to maintain, the cache may cost more than it saves.

clarity.reason: Hit, miss, cache-aside, key, invalidation, TTL, eviction and local/shared are defined with concrete examples and no required unexplained abstraction.

evidence.quote: Sets how long an entry may remain before it expires. A 60-second TTL does not refresh the product every minute; a later miss must load it again.

sourceChecks.claim: Microsoft guidance supports copying frequently reused costly data to reduce source work, with cache storage/management overhead and authoritative source ownership.
Microsoft cache-aside sequence supports application cache lookup then database read/fill on miss, and warns cached copies need not remain consistent.
Microsoft caching guidance assigns application-managed key-value operations and meaningful identity keys; different inputs/private users must not reuse incompatible responses.

Microsoft cache-aside warns consistency is not guaranteed; the stated read-old/commit/delete/refill race is a concrete consequence of separate operations. No false freshness guarantee; authoritative validation avoids that cache copy.

Redis describes memory-based eviction including LRU and noeviction write errors; Microsoft guidance also defines per-entry expiration followed by application refill. TTL neither precludes earlier eviction nor ensures fresh source snapshot.
AWS local/external cache sections support process-local divergent copies versus shared cache/network/operational costs and unavailability scope.
AWS warns cold/unavailable caches flood dependencies, recommends load shedding and caps fallback, and describes coalescing concurrent misses; bounded stale use depends on product rules.
Microsoft guidance and AWS reuse criteria support measuring hit/miss latency and source load and rejecting low-reuse or freshness-incompatible caching.
